ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from Makerere University School of Medicine Research and Ethics Committee (Mak-SOMREC-2025-2110) and administrative clearance from KNRH.

The datasets generated and/or analysed during the current study, including de-identified interview transcripts, are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request, subject to ethical approval for secondary use, given the qualitative and potentially identifying nature of the data.
Twenty participants were recruited in total.
Participants were identified from the family planning clinic register by the clinic in-charge.

Credibility was addressed through interviews in participants' preferred language, open-ended questioning, prolonged engagement, probing, co-facilitation by a female social scientist, member checking (preliminary findings shared with four participants), and regular supervisor debriefs.
All participants provided informed written consent.

Most participants were aged 25-34 years, married, had 3-5 children, and were self-employed, 184 as shown in table 1 188 Lived experiences of long-term users of Cu-T IUDs 189 Participants described a range of positive and negative experiences associated with long-term 190 Cu-T IUD use.
table.formatted: Most participants were aged 25-34 years, married, had 3-5 children, and were self-employed, 184 as shown in table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>  188 Lived experiences of long-term users of Cu-T IUDs 189 Participants described a range of positive and negative experiences associated with long-term 190 Cu-T IUD use.

table.text: Participants were recruited at KNRH, a national referral hospital with specialist care and diagnostic equipment; findings may not be representative of long-term IUD users at lowerlevel health facilities across Uganda.

Participants were identified by the family planning clinic in-charge and nursing staff as women with IUD cards confirming at least two years of use, and were then approached by the PI and research assistants.
Chapter 3 -Sections 3.6 and 3.7 12 Sample Size How many participants were in the study?
The manuscript notes that only women confirmed eligible were recruited; specific numbers who declined at initial approach are not reported.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::
